report:
Conclusion: The evidence supports a specific, interpretable difference: Model B (minus A) pushes the residual stream toward culinary/food-service vocabulary and related commercial/professional terms, especially for early next-token predictions.

Reasoning:
- The L2-norm of the difference is concentrated in late layers (layers ~20–25) and early token positions (pos0–pos1 notably large). That pattern indicates this difference affects the model’s final logit space and therefore next-token choices for the earliest continuation tokens.
- The logit-lens top tokens for the highest-norm (layer,position) cells consistently list cooking/food/restaurant words across many late layers: "restaurant", "Restaurant", "Cooking", "cooking", "Chef", "kitchen", "baking", "Cake", "Cook", "Baked", "microwave", "Kitchen", "Chef", "baker"-type tokens. These appear repeatedly from ~layer 16 onward and dominate in layers 20–25.
- Some other topical tokens (e.g., "dissertation", "doctoral", "chiropractic", "cadmium", "polyurethane", "billionaire", "Michele", "Obama") appear in mid-layers, but the strongest and most consistent signal in the highest-norm late-layer cells is the food/cooking/restaurant cluster. That makes the culinary/restaurant domain the most plausible, coherent interpretation.
- Patchscope continuations were not provided, so interpretation is driven mainly by the logit-lens and norm profile; still the repeated presence of cooking/restaurant tokens across many high-norm cells supports the claim.

Caveats:
- I cannot name an exact training objective or mechanism that produced this difference (e.g., domain-adaptive pretraining on recipe/restaurant corpora vs. fine-tuning), only the behavioral/representational consequence (increased propensity for culinary/restaurant-related tokens).
- There are secondary signals (medical/academic/industrial nouns, some named entities) that indicate other small shifts, but they are less consistent than the cooking/restaurant cluster.
